summary: Power banks are bought device-first: the shopper names a phone or laptop, which fixes the watts one port must deliver (45 W Samsung, 65-100 W laptops, 140 W 16-inch MacBook Pro), then picks a size (10,000 mAh pocket, 20,000-25,000 mAh bag, about 27,000 mAh at the 100 Wh airline line). After that the choice turns on wired or magnetic, a built-in or retractable cable or wall plug, and price tiers near $30, $50 and $100. In the last 60 days Qi2.2 25 W magnetic banks multiplied (Baseus AM71 10,000 mAh on 2026-11-26, UGREEN MagFlow Slim, Anker MagGo 2 Pro), Macworld re-tested laptop banks on 2026-11-04, a HAIARA budget bank was recalled after 600 incident reports, and Black Friday prices moved on several of ours and rivals.

rules: The headline watt figure on a power bank is usually the total across ports. What decides a purchase is the most one port gives one device: UGREEN's 130W bank is 100 W + 30 W, and Baseus's FC41 100W drops to 65 W when a second device joins (Notebookcheck). Apple's support page is the authority for MacBook fast-charge watts, and Macworld's Test Score (two refills of a 14-inch MacBook Pro, percentages added) is the comparable measure of delivered energy for laptop banks. Engadget measured about 60% of label mAh reaching a phone, so mAh is a size class, not a charge count. Watt-hours decide flying: 100 Wh without approval, 100-160 Wh only with the airline's consent. Makers compute Wh at 3.6 V, 3.7 V or 3.2 V (LiFePO4), so mAh figures are not comparable across chemistries. Qi2 means 15 W and Qi2.2 means 25 W; 'magnetic' or 'MagSafe-compatible' alone means neither. Link prices that depend on a code need a cart test dated that week. A price in a reviewer's widget is a lead, not a price. INIU recalled its BI-B41 (CPSC, December 2025); that model is not in the current lineup read here.
